HAZARD COMMUNICATION STANDARD — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

ABOUT THIS HAZARD COMMUNICATION INFORMATION SHEET
This Hazard Communication Standard — Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA regulation requiring employers to inform employees about hazardous chemicals present in the workplace, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC.

It summarizes selected requirements of that regulation: the section's scope and the chemicals and workplaces it covers, the written hazard communication program an employer must develop and maintain, the multi-employer-worksite notification duties that apply where employees of more than one employer share a work area, container labeling requirements, the duty to obtain and maintain safety data sheets (SDSs) and keep them accessible, employee information and training requirements, the limited circumstances in which a specific chemical identity may be withheld as a trade secret, employee and representative access to the written program and SDSs, and selected statutory exemptions from the section's labeling and coverage requirements.

Acme Innovations LLC has identified Pat Morgan as the person responsible for Acme Innovations LLC's written hazard communication program.

This information sheet is not itself Acme Innovations LLC's written hazard communication program, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)'s written-program requirement, and does not determine that any particular chemical, container, label, safety data sheet, or workplace practice of Acme Innovations LLC's is or is not compliant with California law.

WHAT THE STANDARD REQUIRES AND WHICH CHEMICALS IT COVERS
California's Hazard Communication Standard requires manufacturers and importers to classify the hazards of the chemicals they produce or import, requires all employers to provide their employees with information about hazardous chemicals to which the employees may be exposed — through a written hazard communication program, container labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and employee information and training — and requires distributors to transmit the required hazard information to employers. The standard applies to any hazardous chemical that is known to be present in the workplace in a manner under which employees may be exposed under normal conditions of use or in a reasonably foreseeable emergency resulting from workplace operations; it also contains specific provisions for laboratories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section requires manufacturers or importers to classify the hazards of chemicals which they produce or import, and all employers to provide information to their employees about the hazardous chemicals to which they may be exposed, by means of a hazard communication program, labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and information and training."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(1) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(b)(1), scope and application — general requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "This section applies to any hazardous chemical which is known to be present in the work place in such a manner that employees may be exposed under normal conditions of use or in a reasonably foreseeable emergency resulting from work place operations."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(2) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(b)(2), scope and application — coverage trigger (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause states the regulation's own description of its coverage; it does not itself determine whether any particular substance present at any particular workplace meets the regulatory definition of a "hazardous chemical," and it does not restate the section's laboratory-specific provisions, its Proposition 65 cross-reference provisions in subsection (b)(6), or the full list of exempted chemical categories, which are addressed in a separate clause of this information sheet. Classification of a specific chemical requires applying the hazard criteria in the section's Appendix A (health hazards) and Appendix B (physical hazards), which this clause does not reproduce.

THE WRITTEN HAZARD COMMUNICATION PROGRAM
An employer must develop, implement, and maintain at the workplace a written hazard communication program for its employees that at least describes how the standard's requirements for labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and employee information and training will be met. The written program must include a list of the hazardous chemicals known to be present, using a product identifier referenced on the corresponding safety data sheet — a list that may be compiled for the workplace as a whole or for individual work areas — as well as the methods the employer will use to inform employees of the hazards of non-routine tasks, such as cleaning a reactor vessel, and of hazards associated with chemicals contained in unlabeled pipes in the employees' work areas.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Employers shall develop, implement, and maintain at the workplace a written hazard communication program for their employees which at least describes how the criteria specified in sections 5194(f), (g), and (h) for labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and employee information and training will be met"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(e)(1), written hazard communication program requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "A list of the hazardous chemicals known to be present using a product identifier that is referenced on the appropriate safety data sheet (the list may be compiled for the workplace as a whole or for individual work areas)"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1)(A) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(e)(1)(A), required list of hazardous chemicals (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "The methods the employer will use to inform employees of the hazards of non-routine tasks (for example, the cleaning of reactor vessels), and the hazards associated with chemicals contained in unlabeled pipes in their work areas."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1)(B) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(e)(1)(B), non-routine tasks and unlabeled pipes (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause describes the written program's required contents under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1); it does not itself constitute or supply that written program, does not determine whether any particular employer's existing written program is complete or current, and does not address the additional, separate content the same subsection requires for multi-employer workplaces, which is covered in a separate clause of this information sheet.

ADDITIONAL DUTIES AT MULTI-EMPLOYER WORKSITES
Where a workplace has employees of more than one employer present, the written hazard communication program must additionally describe the methods the employer will use to inform any employer sharing the same work area of the hazardous chemicals to which that other employer's employees may be exposed while performing their work, along with any suggestions for appropriate protective measures. The standard specifies that this includes the methods used to provide the other employer access to safety data sheets (or to make them available at a central location), to inform the other employer of precautionary measures needed during normal operations and foreseeable emergencies, and to inform the other employer of the labeling system used at the workplace.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In multi-employer workplaces, the written hazard communication program shall include the methods employers will use to inform any employers sharing the same work area of the hazardous chemicals to which their employees may be exposed while performing their work, and any suggestions for appropriate protective measures"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(2) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(e)(2), multi-employer workplace written program content (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause describes the multi-employer-worksite content requirement in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(2); it does not determine, for any particular jobsite, which employer or employers are legally responsible for a given hazard, and it does not address related but distinct multi-employer safety duties that arise under other Cal/OSHA standards outside section 5194.

LABELING OF CONTAINERS IN THE WORKPLACE
Except as provided by two specific alternatives in the standard, an employer must ensure that each container of hazardous chemicals in the workplace is labeled, tagged, or marked either with the full label information required for shipped containers, or with a product identifier plus words, pictures, symbols, or a combination that provides at least general hazard information, together with other information available to employees under the hazard communication program. An employer may not remove or intentionally deface an existing label on an incoming container of a hazardous chemical unless the container is immediately re-marked with the required information, and workplace labels or other forms of warning must be legible, in English (additional languages may be included), and prominently displayed on the container or otherwise readily available in the work area throughout each work shift.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Workplace labeling. Except as provided in sections 5194(f)(7) and (f)(8) the employer shall ensure that each container of hazardous chemicals in the workplace is labeled, tagged, or marked with either:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(6) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(f)(6), workplace labeling requirement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "The employer shall not remove or intentionally deface existing labels on incoming containers of hazardous chemicals, unless the container is immediately marked with the required information."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(9) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(f)(9), prohibition on removing or defacing incoming labels (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "The employer shall ensure that workplace labels or other forms of warning are legible, in English, and prominently displayed on the container, or readily available in the work area throughout each work shift."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(10) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(f)(10), legibility, language, and display of workplace labels (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause covers workplace container labeling under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(6), (9), and (10); it does not restate the separate, more detailed labeling elements required on containers of hazardous chemicals leaving the workplace under subsection (f)(1)-(5), the stationary-process-container alternative in (f)(7), or the exemption for portable containers intended only for the immediate use of the employee who transfers the chemical, in (f)(8). It does not determine whether a specific label on a specific container currently in use satisfies these requirements.

OBTAINING AND MAINTAINING SAFETY DATA SHEETS
Manufacturers and importers must obtain or develop a safety data sheet (SDS) for each hazardous chemical they produce or import, and every employer must have an SDS for each hazardous chemical it uses. An employer must maintain copies of the required SDSs for each hazardous chemical present in the workplace and must ensure they are readily accessible to employees during each work shift when employees are in their work area(s); the standard permits electronic access and other alternatives to paper copies, so long as no barriers to immediate employee access are created.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Manufacturers and importers shall obtain or develop a safety data sheet for each hazardous chemical they produce or import. Employers shall have a safety data sheet for each hazardous chemical which they use."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(1) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(g)(1), duty to obtain or develop safety data sheets (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "The employer shall maintain copies of the required safety data sheets for each hazardous chemical in the workplace, and shall ensure that they are readily accessible during each work shift to employees when they are in their work area(s)."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(8) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(g)(8), duty to maintain and provide shift-time access to SDSs (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause covers the core SDS-availability duty in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(1), (8), and (9); it does not restate the section's detailed required SDS content and format under (g)(2)-(4), the accuracy and revision-timing duties in (g)(5), the manufacturer/distributor SDS-transmission chain in (g)(6)-(7), or the specific procedure and deadlines an employer must follow when a manufacturer or importer fails to provide a required SDS, set out in (g)(12)-(13).

EMPLOYEE INFORMATION AND TRAINING ON CHEMICAL HAZARDS
An employer must provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into their work area; training may address general classes of hazardous chemicals to the extent appropriate to reasonably foreseeable job exposures, but chemical-specific information must always remain available through labels and safety data sheets. The standard's required training topics include the operations in the employee's work area where hazardous chemicals are present, the location and availability of the written hazard communication program and SDSs, methods to detect a hazardous chemical's presence or release, the physical and health hazards of the workplace chemicals and the protective measures available, and the details of the employer's hazard communication program. Employers must also inform employees of specified rights, including the right to be free from discharge or other discrimination for exercising rights afforded under the Hazardous Substances Information and Training Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Employers shall provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into their work area."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(h)(1) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(h)(1), training trigger — initial assignment and new hazards (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "Against discharge or other discrimination due to the employee's exercise of the rights afforded pursuant to the provisions of the Hazardous Substances Information and Training Act."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(h)(2)(G)(3) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(h)(2)(G)3., anti-discrimination right employees must be informed of (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes the initial/ongoing training trigger and the topic list in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(h)(1)-(2); it does not reproduce every training subtopic verbatim, and it does not restate the separate 30-day timing rule in (h)(3) for informing employees of newly received SDSs that reflect significantly increased risk, which is a distinct, narrower duty this clause does not cover.

TRADE SECRET CHEMICAL IDENTITY AND ITS LIMITS
A manufacturer, importer, or employer may withhold a hazardous chemical's specific chemical identity, or the exact percentage of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet as a trade secret, provided the claim can be supported, the SDS discloses the chemical's properties and effects, the SDS states that the identity or percentage is being withheld as a trade secret, and the specific identity and percentage are made available to health or safety professionals, employees, and designated representatives under the standard's disclosure procedures. Where a treating physician or nurse determines a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity or percentage composition is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer must immediately disclose that trade-secret information to the treating physician or nurse, regardless of any written statement of need or confidentiality agreement. In non-emergency situations, the same information must be disclosed on request to a qualifying health or safety professional, employee, or designated representative who submits a written request meeting the standard's specified content and confidentiality-agreement requirements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The manufacturer, importer or employer may withhold the specific chemical identity of a hazardous chemical, or the exact percentage (concentration) of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet, provided that:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(1) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(i)(1), conditions for withholding a trade-secret chemical identity (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "Where a treating physician or nurse determines that a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity and/or specific percentage of composition of a hazardous chemical is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer shall immediately disclose the specific chemical identity or percentage composition of a trade secret chemical to that treating physician or nurse, regardless of the existence of a written statement of need or a confidentiality agreement."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(2) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(i)(2), mandatory emergency disclosure to a treating physician or nurse (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes the trade-secret withholding conditions and the emergency-disclosure rule in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(1)-(3); it does not restate the detailed non-emergency written-request content requirements in full, the confidentiality-agreement terms in (i)(3)(D)-(E) and (i)(4), the Director's review-and-appeal procedure in (i)(7)-(15) for a denied trade-secret disclosure request, or the outcome of any such dispute for a particular chemical, which this clause does not resolve.

EMPLOYEE AND REPRESENTATIVE ACCESS TO THE PROGRAM AND SDSS
An employer must make its written hazard communication program available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Chief of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Safety data sheets must likewise be made readily available, upon request, to designated representatives and to the Chief, and NIOSH and the employee's physician must be given access to safety data sheets in the same manner. The standard separately defines a "designated representative" as any individual or organization to whom an employee gives written authorization to exercise the employee's rights under the section, with a recognized or certified collective bargaining agent automatically treated as a designated representative without a separate written authorization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The employer shall make the written hazard communication program available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Chief, and NIOSH, in accordance with the requirements of section 3204(e)."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(3) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(e)(3), access to the written program (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "Safety data sheets shall also be made readily available, upon request, to designated representatives, and to the Chief, in accordance with the requirements of section 3204(e). NIOSH and the employee's physician shall also be given access to safety data sheets in the same manner."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(11) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(g)(11), access to safety data sheets (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause covers the access rights in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(3) and (g)(11), together with the "designated representative" definition in subsection (c); it does not describe the recordkeeping-retention timeline for a chemical no longer in use, which the standard cross-references to a separate Cal/OSHA regulation (8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3204) rather than specifying within section 5194 itself, and this clause does not independently verify that separate section's text.

SELECTED EXEMPTIONS FROM THE STANDARD
The standard does not apply to certain categories of chemicals and operations. Among the listed exclusions are consumer products packaged for distribution to, and use by, the general public, provided that employee exposure to the product is not significantly greater than the consumer exposure occurring during the product's principal consumer use, and retail food sale establishments and other retail trade establishments, exclusive of their processing and repair work areas. The standard also addresses work operations where employees only handle hazardous chemicals in sealed containers that are not opened under normal conditions of use, such as in marine cargo handling, warehousing, or transportation — for those operations the general exemption does not fully apply, and the employer instead has narrower, specified duties concerning incoming container labels, safety data sheets, and limited employee training.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Consumer products packaged for distribution to, and use by, the general public, provided that employee exposure to the product is not significantly greater than the consumer exposure occurring during the principal consumer use of the product"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(5)(G) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(G), consumer product exclusion (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "Retail food sale establishments and all other retail trade establishments, exclusive of processing and repair work areas"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(5)(F) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(F), retail establishment exclusion (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  "Work operations where employees only handle chemicals in sealed containers which are not opened under normal conditions of use (such as are found in marine cargo handling, warehousing, or transportation); however, this section does apply to these operations as follows:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(5)(I) (Hazard Communication), 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(I), sealed-container work operations (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/5194.html)
  Known gap: This clause covers three of the several exclusions and exceptions listed in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(4)-(5); it does not reproduce the section's other listed exclusions (pesticides, food/drug/cosmetics, distilled spirits, other consumer-product-agency-regulated items, hazardous waste, tobacco, certain wood products, articles, foods for personal consumption, and pesticide-use compliant with Department of Pesticide Regulation rules), and it does not determine whether any particular product, container, or work operation qualifies for any exclusion or exception — that is a fact-specific classification question the standard leaves to the manufacturer, importer, or employer in the first instance.

Code Regs. § 5194(h)(1)-(2); it does not reproduce every training subtopic verbatim, and it does not restate the separate 30-day timing rule in (h)(3) for informing employees of newly received SDSs that reflect significantly increased risk, which is a distinct, narrower duty this clause does not cover.

expectedJSON.body: A manufacturer, importer, or employer may withhold a hazardous chemical's specific chemical identity, or the exact percentage of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet as a trade secret, provided the claim can be supported, the SDS discloses the chemical's properties and effects, the SDS states that the identity or percentage is being withheld as a trade secret, and the specific identity and percentage are made available to health or safety professionals, employees, and designated representatives under the standard's disclosure procedures. Where a treating physician or nurse determines a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity or percentage composition is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer must immediately disclose that trade-secret information to the treating physician or nurse, regardless of any written statement of need or confidentiality agreement. In non-emergency situations, the same information must be disclosed on request to a qualifying health or safety professional, employee, or designated representative who submits a written request meeting the standard's specified content and confidentiality-agreement requirements.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(i)(1), conditions for withholding a trade-secret chemical identity
citations.quote: The manufacturer, importer or employer may withhold the specific chemical identity of a hazardous chemical, or the exact percentage (concentration) of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet, provided that:

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(i)(2), mandatory emergency disclosure to a treating physician or nurse
citations.quote: Where a treating physician or nurse determines that a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity and/or specific percentage of composition of a hazardous chemical is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer shall immediately disclose the specific chemical identity or percentage composition of a trade secret chemical to that treating physician or nurse, regardless of the existence of a written statement of need or a confidentiality agreement.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause summarizes the trade-secret withholding conditions and the emergency-disclosure rule in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(1)-(3); it does not restate the detailed non-emergency written-request content requirements in full, the confidentiality-agreement terms in (i)(3)(D)-(E) and (i)(4), the Director's review-and-appeal procedure in (i)(7)-(15) for a denied trade-secret disclosure request, or the outcome of any such dispute for a particular chemical, which this clause does not resolve.

expectedJSON.body: An employer must make its written hazard communication program available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Chief of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Safety data sheets must likewise be made readily available, upon request, to designated representatives and to the Chief, and NIOSH and the employee's physician must be given access to safety data sheets in the same manner. The standard separately defines a "designated representative" as any individual or organization to whom an employee gives written authorization to exercise the employee's rights under the section, with a recognized or certified collective bargaining agent automatically treated as a designated representative without a separate written authorization.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(e)(3), access to the written program
citations.quote: The employer shall make the written hazard communication program available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Chief, and NIOSH, in accordance with the requirements of section 3204(e).

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(g)(11), access to safety data sheets
citations.quote: Safety data sheets shall also be made readily available, upon request, to designated representatives, and to the Chief, in accordance with the requirements of section 3204(e). NIOSH and the employee's physician shall also be given access to safety data sheets in the same manner.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause covers the access rights in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(3) and (g)(11), together with the "designated representative" definition in subsection (c); it does not describe the recordkeeping-retention timeline for a chemical no longer in use, which the standard cross-references to a separate Cal/OSHA regulation (8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3204) rather than specifying within section 5194 itself, and this clause does not independently verify that separate section's text.

expectedJSON.body: The standard does not apply to certain categories of chemicals and operations. Among the listed exclusions are consumer products packaged for distribution to, and use by, the general public, provided that employee exposure to the product is not significantly greater than the consumer exposure occurring during the product's principal consumer use, and retail food sale establishments and other retail trade establishments, exclusive of their processing and repair work areas. The standard also addresses work operations where employees only handle hazardous chemicals in sealed containers that are not opened under normal conditions of use, such as in marine cargo handling, warehousing, or transportation — for those operations the general exemption does not fully apply, and the employer instead has narrower, specified duties concerning incoming container labels, safety data sheets, and limited employee training.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(G), consumer product exclusion
citations.quote: Consumer products packaged for distribution to, and use by, the general public, provided that employee exposure to the product is not significantly greater than the consumer exposure occurring during the principal consumer use of the product

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(F), retail establishment exclusion
citations.quote: Retail food sale establishments and all other retail trade establishments, exclusive of processing and repair work areas

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(I), sealed-container work operations
citations.quote: Work operations where employees only handle chemicals in sealed containers which are not opened under normal conditions of use (such as are found in marine cargo handling, warehousing, or transportation); however, this section does apply to these operations as follows:

expectedJSON.gap: This clause covers three of the several exclusions and exceptions listed in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(4)-(5); it does not reproduce the section's other listed exclusions (pesticides, food/drug/cosmetics, distilled spirits, other consumer-product-agency-regulated items, hazardous waste, tobacco, certain wood products, articles, foods for personal consumption, and pesticide-use compliant with Department of Pesticide Regulation rules), and it does not determine whether any particular product, container, or work operation qualifies for any exclusion or exception — that is a fact-specific classification question the standard leaves to the manufacturer, importer, or employer in the first instance.
